title: Cannibalisation
reading_md:
**What it measures.** The sales that other products in the same category lose while one product is on promotion. Shoppers who would have bought the 50-inch TV buy the discounted 55-inch instead, so part of the promoted product's extra volume is taken from its sister products rather than new to Voltmarkt. The classic Voltmarkt case is Earbuds Pro X on deal taking sales from Earbuds Lite.

**Formula (Voltmarkt's convention).**

cannibalised units = SUM over the sister products of (baseline - average weekly units during the promotion) × promotion weeks

cannibalisation rate % = 100 × cannibalised units / incremental units of the promoted product

- Sister products: every product in the promoted product's category that is not in the promotion. A product in the same promotion leaves the set.
- Baseline, as for promo uplift: a product's average weekly units in the 4 weeks before the promotion starts.
- Weekly units come from a zero-filled product by week series, so a week with no sales counts as 0.
- Incremental units of the promoted product = (its average weekly units during the promotion - its baseline) × promotion weeks.
- Every product is measured over the same stores and the same weeks.
- Grain: one promotion.

**Worked example.** A 2-week promotion on the 55-inch TV. It averaged 56 units a week against a baseline of 20, so its incremental units = (56 - 20) × 2 = 72.

| Sister TV | Baseline | Average during the deal | Units lost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50-inch | 15 | 9 | (15 - 9) × 2 = 12 |
| 65-inch | 10 | 7 | (10 - 7) × 2 = 6 |

- Cannibalised units = 12 + 6 = 18.
- Cannibalisation rate = 100 × 18 / 72 = 25.0%: the sister TVs lost 1 unit for every 4 extra units of the 55-inch.
- Net effect on the TV category = 72 - 18 = 54 extra units.

The rate is not a sister product's own drop: the 50-inch fell 40% below its baseline, which is a different number.

**Common mistakes.**

- Comparing different stores or weeks for different products.
- Counting products from other categories. A monitor that sells less during a TV deal is not in the set.
- Leaving another promoted product in the sister set.
- Averaging only the weeks that had sales, which raises the baseline.

**What it does not answer.**

- Whether the promotion made money. A lost sale of a sister product may have earned more margin than the promoted sale that replaced it.
- Sales won from rival shops, or pulled forward from later weeks.

**How managers ask for it.** "Did the Pro X deal just take sales from our other earbuds?" "What's the net category effect?"
